headings.text: 🌳 Decision tree: how do I make this write safe to retry?
🌳 Decision tree: how should a browser reach this API?

notes.html:
Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request

The section answers one question, what does this message promise, and who acts on that promise? A method, status or header is a contract read by caches, proxies and retrying clients who never saw your docs. The through-line: a status code tells the caller whether to retry, so getting it wrong turns one failure into a retry storm.

Concept map

The properties come first because every later note leans on them: they decide what's legal to retry, cache or send across sites.

Green is CORE, blue SUPPORTING, yellow BREADTH. A node with two numbers is two notes, grouped because the section has twelve.

Decision tree: how do I make this write safe to retry?

The binding question is whether the method already gives it to you, so the store is what every other leaf must earn. "Which status code?" belongs to choosing the right code, which owns those trees.

  • PUT to a client URI (safe, idempotent, cacheable): changes if the server must assign ids.
  • Unique constraint (idempotency keys): changes if the same domain key can legitimately repeat.
  • Idempotency-Key (idempotency keys): changes if you can't afford a store on the write path; then fall back to reconciling.
  • Don't auto-retry (timeouts and retries): changes the moment a duplicate starts to cost something.

Decision tree: how should a browser reach this API?

The default is no cross-origin at all, because every preflight and credential rule comes from having two origins.

  • Path route, one origin (CORS): changes if the API must serve other sites.
  • Lax cookie plus CORS (cookies): changes if a sibling subdomain isn't trusted.
  • Short-lived token (cookies): changes if an XSS-exposed token is worse than a third-party cookie.
  • CORS, no credentials (CORS): changes when the data stops being public.

notes.title: HTTP Semantics — Breadth Flashcards
notes.html:
Two topics that hang off HTTP caching and headers.

Content Negotiation and Compression

Stage: message · per request

The client states preferences with Accept, Accept-Encoding and Accept-Language, using q-values, and the server picks one representation. Compression is where the numbers move: gzip is universal, br is the usual choice for text, and zstd is a registered coding (RFC 8878). RFC 9842 adds shared-dictionary dcb and dcz. The rule that bites is Vary: Accept-Encoding: without it, a shared cache can hand one coding to a client that didn't ask for it. Skip already-compressed formats such as JPEG and MP4. HTTP caching owns Vary.

Range Requests and Resumable Downloads

Stage: message · per request

A server advertises Accept-Ranges: bytes, a client sends Range: bytes=0-1023, and the answer is 206 with Content-Range: bytes 0-1023/146515. Out of bounds gets 416. Several ranges come back as multipart/byteranges. If-Range makes a resume safe: send the ETag or date you hold, and a changed file returns the whole 200 instead of stitching two versions together. This is what model-weight downloads and video seeking rely on. A proxy that drops range support makes downloads restart from zero, with no error. Headers owns validators.

notes.title: HTTP Methods & Their Contracts
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9110 §9: Methods · 📜 RFC 5789: PATCH · 📜 RFC 7396: JSON Merge Patch · MDN: HTTP request methods

TL;DR

A method is a one-word contract read by everything on the path. GET reads, POST hands content to the resource to process, PUT makes the URI match the body, PATCH applies a change document, DELETE removes. The real choice is who owns the identifier: the client with PUT, the server with POST, and that decides whether a retry is free.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:request line PUT /things/9f2croute exists? else 404method allowed? else 405 + Allowrun the contractnew: 201, existing: 200 or 204

Recall

Prompt Answer
PUT that creates must return what? 201 (RFC 9110 §9.3.4, MUST); 200 or 204 when it replaces.
What must a 405 carry? Allow, listing the supported methods (§15.5.6).
Which RFC is JSON Merge Patch? RFC 7396, application/merge-patch+json. RFC 7386 is the obsoleted one.

The idea

Two clients create an order and both lose the response. The first sent POST /orders, so the server chose ord_1, and the retry gets ord_2. The second sent PUT /things/9f2c, a URI it chose, so the retry lands on the same resource.

"PUT updates and POST creates" is the belief to drop: both can create. The difference is whose name the thing gets. POST means "you decide what happens and what it's called". PUT means "make this URI hold this". Partial changes add PATCH, which sends instructions and not a state, so PATCH needs a document format and a concurrency story.

The trade: PUT gives you retries by contract and takes server-side id assignment away; POST keeps the ids and makes you build retry safety yourself.

How it works

A method line reaches a proxy, a router and a handler in that order, and each uses it.

Method Contract Body Success Who in the middle acts on it
GET current representation no defined meaning 200, 206 caches store it; prefetchers fire it
HEAD GET's headers, no content no defined meaning 200 caches can refresh entries from it
POST process this content expected 201 + Location, 200, 202 proxies must not auto-retry it
PUT make this URI hold this full state 201, 200, 204 proxies and clients may retry it
PATCH apply this change document patch format 200, 204 treated as non-idempotent
DELETE remove the mapping no defined meaning 204, 200, 202 retried; a repeat 404 is fine
OPTIONS communication options optional 200, 204 + Allow the browser's CORS preflight
QUERY a safe read with a body query content 200 new: support varies (RFC 10008)

A GET body is a real hazard, not a style point: the spec says it "might lead some implementations to reject the request and close the connection", because of request smuggling. QUERY is the honest replacement.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): RFC 9110 defines eight methods, RFC 5789 adds PATCH, RFC 10008 adds QUERY.
  • Changed in RFC 7396 (Oct 2014): JSON Merge Patch replaced RFC 7386. Check any note or tool that still cites the old number.
  • What's next and what won't change: QUERY must spread through proxies before you rely on it. New methods stay rare, so verbs that don't fit become resources.

On the wire

Captured 1 Nov 2026 from our own http.server handler on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15.0, curl 8.7.1), headers trimmed:

PUT /things/9f2c   {"qty":2}
HTTP/1.1 201 Created               # first PUT made it
Location: /things/9f2c

PUT /things/9f2c   {"qty":2}
HTTP/1.1 200 OK                    # second PUT replaced it: same state, new status

POST /orders   {}
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /orders/ord_1            # the server chose the name

PATCH /orders/8f2
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
Allow: GET, HEAD, PUT              # required on a 405

Measure it

  • See it: curl -i -X PUT twice shows 201 then 200; a wrong method shows 405 and Allow; curl -I shows GET's headers with no content.
  • In production: per route, 405 rate and 404 on known paths (client or router drift); destructive routes hit by bot user agents; per client, fields disappearing after a PUT from an old app version.
  • Bounded by: a GET that changes state → no side effects on safe methods; an old client wiping fields with PUT → PATCH with If-Match, or a write that keeps unknown fields.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A method is a contract about intent. GET reads, POST submits for processing, PUT makes a URI hold a state, PATCH applies a change, DELETE removes. What matters in design is identifier ownership: PUT when the client can name the resource, which gives free retries, POST when the server must, which needs idempotency keys. Properties live in the next note.

Q · Mechanism — What does a server do before a handler runs, and why does 405 differ from 404? It matches the URI, then the method on that URI. No route is 404; a route without that method is 405, which MUST send Allow. The difference tells a client which part it got wrong: a 404 sends it hunting for a path, while a 405 tells it what the path supports. Frameworks often do this for you, but hand-rolled routers tend to drop Allow. Python's http.server answers 501 for a method it has no handler for, which is a different claim: the server doesn't recognise it at all.

Q · Trade-off — A 40-field profile: PUT or PATCH? Default to PUT, because full replacement is idempotent and easy to reason about. It fails when an old client fetches, edits two fields and writes back: every field it never learned about is erased. Flip to PATCH when payloads are large or clients own different subsets. Use JSON Merge Patch, keep documents declarative, and pair it with If-Match so concurrent patches can't clobber each other. Merge Patch can't express setting a field to null, since null deletes; JSON Patch (RFC 6902) can, at the cost of an operation list.

Compare

PUT PATCH + Merge Patch PATCH + JSON Patch When you'd pick it
Sends full state changed fields an operation list
Repeat safe yes if the document is declarative no, add to an array repeats
Can set null yes no, null removes the field yes
Pick small resources, one owner large resources, many owners array edits, precise changes

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Methods in the base spec 8 GET…TRACE, including CONNECT spec: RFC 9110 §9.3
PUT created status 201 MUST; 200 or 204 on replace spec: RFC 9110 §9.3.4
405 requirement Allow MUST spec: RFC 9110 §15.5.6

Pitfalls

  • "PUT means update, POST means create"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: CRUD tutorials map them that way.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: both create. PUT returns 201 when it creates at a URI the client named; POST creates where the server chooses.
    ↳ Think instead: the axis is who owns the name, and that axis decides whether a retry is safe.
  • Not the same: PUT vs PATCH
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both change an existing resource, and many APIs accept partial bodies on PUT.
    ↳ Difference: PUT sends the state you want; PATCH sends instructions. A partial PUT breaks the idempotent-replace contract clients rely on.
    ↳ Think instead: state or instructions? State is PUT; instructions are PATCH with a media type.
  • Don't reach for PATCH without a concurrency story.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's smaller on the wire and feels more precise.
    ↳ What goes wrong: two partial updates race, both succeed and a field silently loses. RFC 5789 warns some patch formats corrupt a resource without a known base.
    ↳ Do instead: send If-Match with the ETag you read, as headers shows.
  • Don't invent a method.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: APPROVE /orders/1 reads well, and HTTP allows extension methods.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a middlebox or framework that doesn't know it may reject it, and only some networks fail.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: POST /orders/1/approval, an action modelled as a resource.
  • Shelf life: the method contracts are durable. QUERY support is what will move.

Connections

Path:HTTP as a protocolmethodssafe, idempotent, cacheable
  • Builds on HTTP as a protocol: the request line these occupy.
  • Used by REST: resources get their verbs from here.
  • Owned elsewhere: safe, idempotent, cacheable owns the properties; choosing the right code owns error codes.
  • Composes with headers: If-Match makes partial updates safe.

notes.title: Safe vs Idempotent vs Cacheable
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9110 §9.2: Common Method Properties · 📜 RFC 5789: PATCH · 📜 RFC 10008: QUERY · MDN: Idempotent · MDN: Safe (HTTP methods)

TL;DR

Three separate questions, not one scale. Safe: may I send this at all without asking for a change? Idempotent: may I send it again? Cacheable: may I reuse the reply? The method answers all three before anyone reads your code, so every cache, proxy and retrying client acts on them. The spec turns one of them into a hard rule: a proxy must not automatically retry a non-idempotent request.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:request failssafe method? retryidempotent? retry, same effectPOST or PATCH? a proxy must not retrya client may only with proofproof is a client-owned id or an idempotency key

Recall

Prompt Answer
Idempotent but not safe? PUT and DELETE.
DELETE twice gives 204 then 404. Idempotent? Yes. The property is about intended effect, not the response.
Is PATCH idempotent? Not by definition. A given patch can be, so it's the document's property.
Who is forbidden to retry a POST? A proxy: MUST NOT (RFC 9110 §9.2.2). A client: SHOULD NOT without proof.
Cacheable with no explicit freshness? GET and HEAD. POST needs explicit freshness; PUT, DELETE never.
Draw by hand: a lost response, retried Client → proxy → API; applied, connection drops; PUT retried safely; POST surfaces 502.

The idea

A client sends POST /orders. The API writes the row, and the connection drops before the response gets back. Nobody on the client side can tell "never arrived" from "applied, reply lost", and no amount of waiting will tell them. If anything resends it, that's a second order.

Now send the same order as PUT /orders/9f2c with a client-chosen id. The state after two sends equals the state after one, so anyone may resend without asking you. That is the whole purpose of the property: the spec says idempotent methods are distinguished "because the request can be repeated automatically if a communication failure occurs before the client is able to read the server's response".

So the method is a promise to strangers. A proxy can't read your handler and doesn't try: it reads PUT and acts. Break the promise in code, with a DELETE that fires a webhook every time, and the middle will still retry it.

The trade: declaring the property lets the whole path recover from failures for free, and you pay by keeping the promise in every handler, because nothing enforces it.

How it works

The same failure twice. The method, not the server's state, decides what the proxy may do next.

The arrow that matters is ④: the proxy hands the problem back, because only something that can prove the retry is harmless may repeat it.

Rule What actually happens
Safe implies idempotent, one way GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE are safe, so idempotent too. PUT and DELETE are idempotent and change state.
Cacheable is a separate axis PUT is idempotent and uncacheable. POST is rarely cacheable: it needs explicit freshness and a matching Content-Location, and then serves only a later GET or HEAD.
The property describes intent Logging, metrics and revision history on a GET don't break safety. The client didn't ask for them.
Who in the middle acts on it Crawlers and prefetchers fire safe methods unprompted; caches store by method; L7 proxies retry by method; clients retry by method.
Retry rule Client SHOULD NOT retry non-idempotent requests without knowing it's harmless. Proxy MUST NOT. A client SHOULD NOT retry a failed automatic retry.

Evolution

Lineage:1997 RFC 2068 names safe and idempotent2010 RFC 5789 adds PATCH, neither2022 RFC 9110 consolidates them in §9.22026 RFC 10008 adds QUERY, safe with a body
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): the definitions are stable, and every HTTP client and proxy keys retries on them.
  • Changed in RFC 10008 (Jun 2026): before QUERY, a search with a large body had to be a POST, which forfeits retry and caching. QUERY is safe, idempotent and cacheable with the content in the key.
  • What's next and what won't change: QUERY support will spread through proxies. The rule stays: the middle only knows what the method says.

On the wire

Captured 1 Nov 2026 from our own http.server handler on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15.0, curl 8.7.1). A second DELETE after a retry:

DELETE /things/9f2c
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content           # gone

DELETE /things/9f2c               # the retry of a lost response
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found            # different response, same resulting state

Break it: a handler commits, then drops the connection without answering. --retry-all-errors is a method-blind retrier, the behaviour the spec forbids in a proxy.

curl --retry 1 --retry-delay 0 --retry-all-errors -X POST -d '{"sku":"A"}' $U/lost/order
curl --retry 1 --retry-delay 0 --retry-all-errors -X PUT  -d '{"sku":"A"}' $U/lost/thing
# look for: rows the server holds after each command
# naive belief predicts: one row each, because "the first attempt failed"

Run on the same lab: both commands exit 0 with 200, and each path was hit twice. POST left 2 rows; PUT left 1. The client saw identical success, so only the server's state shows the duplicate.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -i the same PUT or DELETE twice, then GET: the state matches a single send even when the status differs.
  • In production: per route, count duplicate writes by client reference; per proxy, read its retry counter split by method (any non-idempotent retry is a config bug); per request, attempts against unique requests.
  • Bounded by: a duplicate side effect from a retried write → method discipline, then a client-owned id or an idempotency key; a proxy allowed to retry POST → leave it off, as in the nginx default.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: They're three independent properties. Safe means the client isn't asking for a change, idempotent means repeating has the same intended effect, cacheable means a stored reply may be reused. GET is all three; PUT and DELETE are idempotent only; POST is none by default. It matters because caches and proxies act on the method alone, and RFC 9110 forbids proxies from auto-retrying non-idempotent requests.

Q · Mechanism — Why is PATCH the awkward one? RFC 5789 says PATCH is neither safe nor idempotent, and adds that a request can be issued so that it is. A merge patch setting {"status":"shipped"} converges; an increment or an array append doesn't. So a proxy can't assume anything, and idempotency becomes a property of the document, which can change with a payload. To make a PATCH retryable, keep it declarative or pair it with If-Match, so a replay fails with 412 rather than applying twice. HTTP methods owns the choice between PUT and PATCH.

Q · Trade-off — When is PUT to a client-chosen id better than POST plus a key? PUT /orders/{uuid} needs no store, no expiry and no race: the method's contract does the work. It costs server-side id assignment, so it fails where ids must be sequential or issued by a downstream system. A natural unique key beats both when the operation already has identity, such as an invoice number. POST with an idempotency key is what's left when you need server-issued ids. Pick in that order, because each step adds a moving part.

Q · Failure — Customers report duplicate charges after a load balancer change. What happened? Something now retries a non-idempotent method: a POST that succeeded but lost its response was resent, and the duplicate needs only one dropped reply, so load is irrelevant. Confirm by matching two backend writes to one client request id, then check the proxy's retry config for method scoping. Fix it by scoping retries to idempotent methods or keyed requests. What runs out is the customer's trust, not a resource: the dashboard shows healthy 201s, and refunds are the symptom.

Q · Design — Design the write path for an irreversible side effect, like a payment. The binding constraint is that a timeout is ambiguous, so assume at-least-once arrival and design for one effect. The client owns a key per logical operation, and the service makes it atomic before the side effect (idempotency keys). The gateway passes POST through without retrying, and one layer, the client, owns retries (retries done right). Watch fingerprint mismatches on keys first. The pattern is placed in resilience patterns.

Compare

Method Safe Idempotent Cacheable When you'd pick it
GET, HEAD a read
OPTIONS, TRACE capabilities, diagnostics
QUERY , content in the key a read too big for a URL
PUT, DELETE replace or remove at a known URI
POST explicit freshness + Content-Location the server decides what happens
PATCH not by definition explicit freshness + Content-Location a partial change

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Safe methods in the base spec 4 GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE spec: RFC 9110 §9.2.1
Idempotent methods in the base spec 6 the safe four + PUT, DELETE spec: RFC 9110 §9.2.2
Cacheable methods in the base spec GET, HEAD, POST POST only with explicit freshness and Content-Location spec: RFC 9110 §9.2.3, §9.3.3
Rows after a lost response and a blind retry POST 2, PUT 1 our handler, one retry measured: curl 8.7.1, 1 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "Idempotent means the same response every time"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: math's idempotence sounds like "same output", and a retry that returns something new looks broken.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the property is the intended effect on the server. DELETE gives 204 then 404, and the spec says the response "might differ".
    ↳ Think instead: compare state, not status. Don't "fix" a correct 404 into a 204 for things that never existed.
  • Not the same: safe vs idempotent
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: every safe method is idempotent, so the two look like one idea of "harmless".
    ↳ Difference: safe says the client requests no change; idempotent allows a change, once. The arrow runs one way.
    ↳ Think instead: safe answers "may I send it?"; idempotent answers "may I send it again?" PUT passes only the second.
  • "GET can't have side effects"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "safe" sounds like a guarantee from the server.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it describes what the client asked for. Nothing enforces it, and crawlers and prefetchers fire GETs unprompted, so GET /items/5/delete gets exercised by a bot.
    ↳ Think instead: safe is a promise you keep. Logging is fine; a state change the client didn't ask for is a bug.
  • "Idempotent by spec means idempotent in my service"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: you used DELETE, and the RFC lists it.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a handler that fires a webhook or decrements a counter on every call has broken the promise, and clients still retry on it.
    ↳ Think instead: the method is what you promised, and the handler is what you delivered. Test a double send.
  • Not the same: idempotent vs ordered
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are filed under "safe writes".
    ↳ Difference: idempotency makes one write's duplicate harmless. Two different writes racing is a lost update, and neither a key nor PUT stops it.
    ↳ Think instead: duplicates need identity; overwrites need a precondition.
  • Don't add a dedup store where PUT would do.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: idempotency keys are the pattern everyone copies from payments.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you take on a new write-path dependency, an expiry job and a race to get right, for a resource whose id the client could have chosen.
    ↳ Do instead: a client-owned id with PUT, or a unique constraint on a natural key, before any key table.
  • Shelf life: the definitions are durable. QUERY support and each proxy's retry defaults are what will move.

Connections

Path:HTTP methodssafe, idempotent, cacheablestatus codesidempotency keys
  • Builds on HTTP methods: each method's contract, classified here.
  • Used by REST: its uniform interface is these three properties.
  • Owned elsewhere: exactly-once owns why delivery can't be exactly once; HTTP caching owns directives.
  • Bounded by idempotency keys: what makes a POST provably safe to resend.
  • Decided in resilience patterns: where a service places its retries.
  • Drilled in idempotent POST and idempotent endpoint.

notes.title: Status Codes — the Practical Map
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9110 §15: Status Codes · 📜 RFC 6585: 428, 429, 431, 511 · MDN: HTTP response status codes · AWS: ALB troubleshooting · Envoy: access log response flags

TL;DR

The class is the contract: 2xx worked, 3xx look elsewhere, 4xx change the request, 5xx the same request may work later. Retry layers, circuit breakers, caches and alerts read that without opening your body. The second thing to read is who emitted it. A 502, 503 or 504 usually comes from a hop, so the app may have logged nothing.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:read the class4xx: change the request5xx: who emitted it?app logged it: 500, its bugno app log: a hop502 bad reply503 not attempted504 no timely reply

Recall

Prompt Answer
502 vs 503 vs 504 in the RFC? invalid upstream response · temporarily unable · no timely upstream response.
Which is ambiguous for a write? 504: the upstream may still be doing the work.
Must 201 carry Location? No. Without it, the target URI names the resource.
Which codes keep the method on redirect? 307, 308: MUST NOT change it.
Must 401, 405 carry what? WWW-Authenticate; Allow. Both MUST.
Draw by hand: whose log do I open? App logged it? its bug. If not: 502 lifecycle, 503 pool, 504 latency.

The idea

Three worked decisions, situation → checks → answer → defence:

  • POST /v1/charges moved to a new path, and clients now see 405. Which redirect? Did the method survive? 301 turns a POST into a GET in browsers and curl. Answer: 308. Defence: it's permanent and MUST NOT change the method, so the body arrives.
  • Dashboard spike: 503, and the app log is empty. Who emitted it? Was anything attempted? Is there a pool with healthy members? Answer: the proxy, with nowhere to send it. Defence: no app log means no attempt, so a write is safe to retry here, unlike 504.
  • A job endpoint returns 200 {"ok":true} and clients read a result that doesn't exist. Is the work finished? Answer: 202. Defence: the spec says the response "ought to describe the request's current status and point to" a monitor, so the client has somewhere to go.

The trade: precise codes cost nothing to send and buy correct behaviour from software you don't own; vague ones are paid for in retries and in time spent in the wrong log.

How it works

The table you recall under pressure. "Retry?" means the same bytes, with backoff, for a method that allows it.

Code Says Usually from Retry? Contract detail
100 101 go on · switching origin n/a WebSocket upgrade is 101
103 early hints origin, edge n/a RFC 8297
200 it worked origin no heuristically cacheable
201 created origin no Location, or the target URI names it
202 accepted, not done origin poll point to a monitor (jobs)
204 nothing to send origin no no content
206 part of it origin, cache n/a range card
301 302 moved · found origin, edge follow POST may become GET
303 see other origin follow switch to GET on purpose
304 your copy is good origin, cache n/a a validator answer, no content
307 308 same, method kept origin, edge follow MUST NOT change method
400 can't parse origin, edge no fix the bytes
401 who are you? origin, gateway with credentials MUST send WWW-Authenticate
403 refused origin, gateway, WAF no may hide as 404
404 no such thing origin, edge no heuristically cacheable
405 method unsupported origin no MUST send Allow
406 415 can't produce · can't read origin no negotiation
408 request not finished proxy, server client MAY
409 conflicts with state origin after resolving body explains
410 gone for good origin no heuristically cacheable
412 428 precondition failed · required origin re-read first headers
413 414 431 too large proxy, server no body · URI · headers
416 range not satisfiable origin no
421 wrong connection origin, gateway yes, new connection any method (§15.5.20)
422 parsed, can't process origin no fix the values
425 too early terminator MUST, without 0-RTT early data
429 too many limiter after Retry-After rate limiting
451 legally unavailable origin no RFC 7725
500 origin failed app maybe unspecific
501 not implemented origin no heuristically cacheable
502 invalid upstream reply proxy yes, if idempotent see below
503 can't handle it now proxy or app yes MAY send Retry-After
504 no timely upstream reply proxy if idempotent work may still run

Whose log do you open? The answer depends on where the code came from, so split that first; the default leaf is your own bug.

The middle owns the second column, and vendors draw the lines differently, so name the proxy before you reason from the code.

Rule What actually happens
The RFC is broader than the triad 502 and 504 are about a gateway; 503 is any temporary inability, so an app or limiter may send it.
ALB, as of Nov 2026 502: RST or FIN with a request outstanding, malformed reply. 503: no registered targets. 504: no connection or no response in time.
Envoy, as of Nov 2026 Upstream connection termination is flag UC with 503, not 502. Timeout is UT with 504.
Heuristic caching 200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 308, 404, 405, 410, 414, 501: a cache may reuse them with no explicit freshness (§15.1).
Redirect limits Fetch fails after 20 redirects; curl's -L default is 50.

Evolution

Lineage:1997 RFC 20682012 RFC 6585 adds 4292015 RFC 7538 adds 3082018 RFC 8470 adds 4252022 RFC 9110 absorbs 308, 421, 422
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): the registry grows slowly and the classes are fixed.
  • Changed in RFC 9110 (Jun 2022): 422 moved in from WebDAV and became Unprocessable Content; 413 became Content Too Large; 308 no longer needs RFC 7538, which it obsoletes.
  • What's next and what won't change: vendors keep adding private codes, like ALB's 460 and 463. The class meaning stays.

On the wire

Our own proxy on 127.0.0.1 in front of our own app, a 0.2 s upstream timeout, captured 1 Nov 2026 (Python 3.15.0, curl 8.7.1). It shows the meanings, not any vendor's mapping:

GET /reset    # the app closes the connection without replying
HTTP/1.1 502 Bad Gateway      # app access log: an entry, then nothing
GET /none     # the proxy has no healthy upstream
HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
Retry-After: 5                # app access log: no entry at all
GET /slow     # the app takes 0.6 s
HTTP/1.1 504 Gateway Timeout  # returned at 0.20 s, and the app finished anyway

Break it: does a redirect keep your POST? A /target handler echoes what arrives.

for c in 301 302 303 307 308; do curl -s -L -d amount=5 $U/moved/$c; done
curl -s -L -X POST -d amount=5 $U/moved/301
# look for: which codes deliver the POST and its body
# naive belief predicts: every redirect keeps the request; only permanence differs

Run with curl 8.7.1: 301, 302 and 303 gave GET body=''; 307 and 308 gave POST body='amount=5'. The surprise is the last line: forcing -X POST through a 301 sent POST body='', so the method survived and the body didn't.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -si -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}', then the hop's header (server, via); in devtools, a redirect's method column.
  • In production: per code, per emitting hop, never one 5xx rate; on ALB, HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count against HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count; 5xx at the edge with no app log means a hop.
  • Bounded by: a retry storm from a mislabelled code → the choice rules; a cached error outliving the fault → an explicit lifetime on 404 and 410; an unsafe redirect → 307 or 308.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: The class is a contract with every machine on the path: 4xx means change the request, 5xx means it might work later. So a 500 for a validation error makes every retry layer resend something that can't succeed. On incidents I split by code and by emitting hop first: 502, 503 and 504 usually come from a proxy, and the app log being empty is itself the clue.

Q · Mechanism — Which of the three means nothing was attempted? Usually 503 from a proxy: no healthy target or a limit rejected the request before dispatch, so the app never saw it, as the capture's missing log entry shows. 504 is the opposite: it was dispatched and may still be running, which is why it's ambiguous for writes. 502 sits between, because the upstream was reached and may have applied the write before the connection died. So retrying a POST after a proxy's 503 is usually safe; after 502 or 504 it needs a key. Confirm per proxy, since Envoy reports connection termination as 503.

Q · Trade-off — 301 or 308 for a path rename? For an API, 308, because a 301 lets clients drop the body. For a pure page move, 301 is fine, and older clients know it. The cost of either is that they're heuristically cacheable, so a mistaken permanent redirect outlives the deploy that made it. During a migration use 307 until you're sure, then promote. 303 is the deliberate opposite: post, then redirect to a GET, so a browser refresh doesn't resubmit.

Q · Failure — 502s appear on every deploy, about one per pod. Why? A pod closes or is killed while the proxy has a request on that connection; ALB's docs name exactly this, "the target closed the connection" with a request outstanding, and a keep-alive shorter than the balancer's idle timeout. What runs out is the proxy's assumption that a pooled connection is still good. Confirm with elb_status_code against an empty target_status_code in the access log, and pod termination timestamps. Fix with graceful draining and an upstream keep-alive longer than the proxy's idle timeout.

Q · Design — Who may emit what in a request path you design? App code owns 2xx, 4xx and 500. The edge and mesh own 502, 504 and their own 503. Anything else needs a reason: an app returning 502 is hiding a proxy, and an edge returning 422 is reading bodies it shouldn't. Retry-After must come from what knows the recovery time. Then watch per-code, per-hop rates first. For availability SLOs, count 5xx only, and track 429 as saturation. Placement belongs with the API gateway; the service view is resilience patterns.

Compare

Redirect Permanent Method kept When you'd pick it
301 yes may become GET a page moved for good
302 no may become GET legacy temporary move
303 no becomes GET post, then show the result
307 no yes temporary move of an API
308 yes yes permanent move of an API

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Fetch redirect limit 20 then a network error spec: Fetch Standard, HTTP-redirect fetch
curl -L limit 50 --max-redirs default default (as of Nov 2026): curl 8.7.1 man page
ALB connection and TLS timeout to a target 10 s then 504 default (as of Nov 2026): ALB docs
Timing of a 504 from our proxy 0.20 s 0.2 s upstream timeout measured: curl 8.7.1, 1 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "4xx is the client's fault, 5xx is the server's"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the RFC names them client error and server error.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: what matters is what to do next. 429 is a 4xx you should retry, and S3 throttles one caller with 503.
    ↳ Think instead: read the class as an instruction: change the request, or try again.
  • Not the same: 502 vs 504
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both come from a proxy, and both mean the upstream let it down.
    ↳ Difference: 502 got something invalid or lost the connection; 504 got nothing in time.
    ↳ Think instead: 502 is connection lifecycle, 504 is latency. They send you to different dashboards.
  • "201 must carry Location"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: most APIs do, and old notes say MUST.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: §15.3.2 says the resource is named by Location "or, if no Location header field is received, by the target URI", as with a PUT.
    ↳ Think instead: send Location when the server chose the name, because the client has no other way to know it.
  • "304 is a redirect"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it sits in the 3xx class.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: nothing moved. It answers a conditional request by saying your stored copy still holds, with no content.
    ↳ Think instead: 304 is a cache answer, owned by HTTP caching.
  • Don't return 200 with an error in the body.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the transport "succeeded", and one handler path is simpler.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every proxy, retry layer and dashboard sees success, and a cache may store the failure.
    ↳ Do instead: the honest code plus one error body from REST API design.
  • Don't invent or overload a code.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a custom number feels more precise than a body field.
    ↳ What goes wrong: intermediaries treat an unknown code as its class (§15), so the precision reaches nobody.
    ↳ Do instead: the standard code, with a stable machine-readable code in the body.
  • Shelf life: classes and RFC rules are durable. Vendor mappings and private codes change; re-check them against the Landscape.

Connections

Path:safe, idempotent, cacheablestatus codeschoosing the right code
  • Builds on HTTP methods: 405 and redirect behaviour depend on them.
  • Used by timeouts and retries: the retry table reads this one.
  • Owned elsewhere: choosing the right code owns which one to send; triage playbooks own incident steps.
  • Bounded by idempotency keys: what makes a 502 or 504 on a write retryable.
  • Measured by the metrics that matter: RED per hop.
  • Decided in the API gateway: which hop emits which code.

notes.title: Choosing the Right Status Code
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9110 §15.5: Client Error · 📜 RFC 9110 §13.2: Evaluation of Preconditions · 📜 RFC 6585: 428 and 429 · MDN: status codes · GitHub: REST API troubleshooting

TL;DR

Picking a code is a short series of yes/no questions in a fixed order, not a lookup. Could I read it? Who is asking? May they know this exists? Is this caller over quota? Is their version current? Would it work against any state? The answer programs somebody else's retry loop, so a wrong 500 resends what can't succeed, and a wrong 403 confirms what you meant to hide.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:parse ─400credentials ─401may they know? ─404permitted ─403quota ─429preconditions ─428, 412meaning ─422current state ─409200

Recall

Prompt Answer
The question separating 400 from 422? Did the bytes parse? No is 400.
401 vs 403? No valid credentials is 401. Credentials insufficient is 403.
409 vs 422? Could the same request work after state changes? Yes is 409.
412 vs 428? 412: your precondition is stale. 428: you sent none and it's required.
429 vs 503? This caller's rate, or the server's ability to serve anyone.
Draw by hand: the two trees Who is asking: 400, 401, 404, 403. Can it work now: 429, 503, 428, 412, 422, 409.

The idea

Four worked decisions, situation → checks in order → answer → defence:

  • Tenant t_09 asks for t_42's document. Parsed? yes. Credentials? valid. May they know it exists? no. Answer: 404. Defence: RFC 9110 §15.5.4 allows it, and a 403 would answer an id-scanning loop. Log the real reason against a request id.
  • A valid JSON body has owner: "tuesday". Parsed? yes. Authorised and current? yes. Against any state? still wrong. Answer: 422. Defence: 400 sends the client to its serialiser, 422 to the value.
  • A valid edit of a document locked for review. Fine in itself, wrong right now. Answer: 409. Defence: the same bytes will work when the lock clears, which is what §15.5.10 means by a conflict the user might resolve.
  • A database is down, and every caller fails. Not this caller's rate. Answer: 503 with Retry-After. Defence: 500 says nothing about waiting, and 429 sends every client to audit its quota.

The trade: the questions cost a shared helper and some discipline across handlers, and they buy correct behaviour from every retry layer and SDK you'll never read.

How it works

First, who is asking. Permission runs before existence, so you never confirm what you wouldn't serve. The default leaf is carrying on.

Then, can it work now. RFC 9110 §13.2.1 fixes where preconditions go: after your normal checks, "just before" processing the content, so 412 comes before a value check.

Each pair below has one deciding question. A gateway may answer 401 or 429 before your code runs, so these trees describe the whole path, not one handler.

Pair The deciding question Left when Right when What the client does
400 vs 422 Did the bytes parse? syntax broken syntax fine, values wrong fix the encoding, or fix the field
401 vs 403 Are credentials missing or invalid? yes valid but insufficient authenticate, or stop
403 vs 404 May the caller know it exists? yes no ask for access, or nothing to learn
404 vs 410 Do you assert it's permanently gone? no yes maybe later, or drop the link
409 vs 412 Did a precondition fail? no: other state conflict yes: their version is stale resolve, or re-read and rebase
409 vs 422 Could the same bytes work later? yes no wait or resolve, or edit
412 vs 428 Did they send a precondition? yes, stale no, required re-read, or add If-Match
429 vs 503 This caller, or everyone? this caller everyone back off, or everyone waits
415 vs 422 Is the media type readable? no yes change Content-Type, or the value

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): the codes are settled; 400 vs 422 remains a house rule, and RFC 9457 is the standard error body.
  • Changed in RFC 9110 (Jun 2022): 422 is now in the base spec, not just WebDAV, so choosing it no longer needs a footnote.
  • What's next and what won't change: the Idempotency-Key draft recommends 422 for a reused key and 409 for one in flight. The rule stays: the code routes, the body explains.

On the wire

Eight PUTs to one document from our own http.server handler on 127.0.0.1, captured 1 Nov 2026 (Python 3.15.0, curl 8.7.1). The document belongs to t_42 at "v7", and starts locked.

PUT /docs/d_9f2c  (no credentials)                 # → 401, WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="docs"
PUT  Bearer t_42  {oops                            # → 400, can't read it
PUT  Bearer t_09  {}                               # → 404, X-Request-ID: rq_5a1c
PUT  Bearer t_42  {}                               # → 428, no precondition
PUT  If-Match: "v6"  {}                            # → 412, someone wrote v7
PUT  If-Match: "v7"  {"owner":"tuesday"}           # → 422, parsed, wrong value
PUT  If-Match: "v7"  {"owner":"a@b.io"}            # → 409, locked for review
PUT  (same bytes, lock released)                   # → 200, ETag: "v8"

The last two lines are the 409 test: identical bytes, different state, different answer.

Break it: a validation failure labelled 500 meets a client that retries.

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' --retry 2 --retry-delay 0 $U/flaky500   # wrong label
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' --retry 2 --retry-delay 0 $U/bad422     # right label
# look for: how many requests the server counted for each
# naive belief predicts: one each, because the code is only a label for humans

Run with curl 8.7.1, whose --retry treats 408, 429, 500, 502, 503 and 504 as transient: /flaky500 was hit 3 times, /bad422 once. The server's work tripled from one wrong digit, and this client had one retry layer.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -si each branch; a tenant test should show a 404 byte-identical to one for a missing document, apart from the request id.
  • In production: per route, attempts against unique requests split by code: anything above 1 on a 4xx means someone retries the hopeless; per tenant, 404 rate as a scan signal.
  • Bounded by: a retry storm from a wrong 5xx → one shared error helper, linted; an existence leak → a tenant-scoped lookup that can only return 404.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: It's a sequence of questions, in order. Did it parse: 400. Credentials: 401. May they know it exists: 404 over 403. Quota: 429. Precondition: 428 or 412. Meaning: 422. Current state: 409. The order matters because permission before existence stops leaks. And every machine downstream acts on the answer, so a wrong 500 is someone else's retry storm.

Q · Mechanism — Why 404 instead of 403 for another tenant's object, and what does it cost? A 403 tells an id-scanning loop that the id exists, and sequential ids leak volume too. 404 answers the same either way, and §15.5.4 explicitly lets an origin server hide existence this way. GitHub does this for private repositories. The cost lands on support: "it 404s but I can see it in the UI" could be the wrong tenant, a revoked grant or a deletion. So return a request id and log the true reason against it. Inside one trust boundary, 403 is better, since the object's existence isn't the secret.

Q · Trade-off — Should an API split 400 and 422? Split them only if you can enforce it. The split helps a client tell "fix your serialiser" from "fix this field", and it's what RFC 9110 describes. But half the handlers using each for the same failure is worse than always 400, because a client can code against a blunt rule and not an inconsistent one. The tipping point is whether one helper or framework owns validation. If it does, split; if each team hand-rolls errors, pick 400, write it down and put the detail in the body.

Q · Failure — Error budget burns, and every breaker opens, on a day with no outage. Why? One route answers 500 for a validation failure, so retry layers resend it and breakers count it. What runs out is your budget and dependency capacity, spent on requests that were never the server's fault. The opposite bug is quieter: a 400 for a transient dependency failure makes clients give up on what a retry would have fixed. Confirm by splitting 5xx by route and comparing attempts with unique requests. Fix the code in the handler, not the alert.

Q · Design — Design the error contract for a public multi-tenant API. One envelope everywhere, RFC 9457 application/problem+json, owned by REST API design: stable type, status, title, a request id. Clients branch on the type, never on prose. Validation returns every failing field at once, so one fix isn't one round trip. Tenant checks live in one lookup that can only answer 404. Watch per-tenant 404 and per-route 5xx, and version your types like any contract. For the path view, see who may emit what and service communication.

Compare

Your limit Code Retry-After When you'd pick it
per caller quota 429 yes one caller, others fine
whole service overloaded 503 yes everyone is affected
a required dependency down 503 yes you're down, but it should pass
a request that can never fit 413 or 422 no retrying can't help
a billing cap 402 or 403 no needs a human, by your docs

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Requests for one wrong 500 3, against 1 for 422 curl --retry 2, one layer measured: curl 8.7.1, 1 Nov 2026
WWW-Authenticate on 401 MUST at least one challenge spec: RFC 9110 §15.5.2
404 to hide a forbidden resource MAY origin server's choice spec: RFC 9110 §15.5.4
Precondition timing after normal checks, before content a 4xx from checks wins spec: RFC 9110 §13.2.1
Weak If-Match never matches strong comparison is a MUST spec: RFC 9110 §13.1.1

Pitfalls

  • "403 is the secure answer"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it means "forbidden", which sounds like the strict choice.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it confirms the object exists, so a loop over ids reads each 403 as a hit, and the leak appears on no dashboard.
    ↳ Think instead: 404 unless the caller already knows it exists, as with something shared and later revoked.
  • Not the same: 409 vs 412
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both mean "the state moved under you".
    ↳ Difference: 412 is a precondition the client wrote evaluating false; 409 is any other conflict, which the body must explain.
    ↳ Think instead: prefer the precondition. It names exactly what changed.
  • "401 means not logged in, so a redirect is fine"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: browser login flows redirect, and APIs copy them.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a 401 MUST carry WWW-Authenticate, and a 302 hands a generic client an HTML login page it reads as success.
    ↳ Think instead: APIs answer 401 with a challenge; only a browser flow redirects.
  • "429 always comes with a real rate limit, 503 never does"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the table above reads that way.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: S3 signals 503 Slow Down for a request rate, and GitHub returns 403 or 429 for rate limits.
    ↳ Think instead: design by the table, but consume by the docs. A client reads the provider's rules, and Retry-After.
  • Don't emit 503 for one tenant's quota.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one code for "we can't serve you" is less work.
    ↳ What goes wrong: breakers and retry layers count a healthy service as failing, and hide which tenant caused it.
    ↳ Do instead: 429 with Retry-After, scoped to the caller, as in rate limiting.
  • Don't build a code matrix when one rule would do.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: more precise codes feel more correct.
    ↳ What goes wrong: inconsistent handlers make clients guess, and that's worse than a blunt rule.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: 400 for all client input errors, the detail in the body, until one helper owns validation.
  • Shelf life: the questions and RFC rules are durable. Provider-specific throttling codes change.

Connections

Path:status codeschoosing the right codeheaders
  • Builds on status codes: the table this decides against.
  • Owned elsewhere: REST API design owns the error envelope; headers owns If-Match.
  • Bounded by timeouts and retries: the retry loop your code choice programs.
  • Used by REST: 412, 409, 422 and 202 in use.
  • Decided in service communication: what a service boundary promises its callers.

notes.title: Headers That Matter
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9110 §13: Conditional Requests · 📜 RFC 7239: Forwarded · MDN: If-Match · MDN: X-Forwarded-For

TL;DR

Headers are how a request talks to everything except your handler: caches, proxies, limiters, browsers. Nine fields do most of the work. The one people miss is If-Match: an idempotency key stops the same write twice, and only a precondition stops two different writes overwriting each other. The one people over-trust is X-Forwarded-For, whose leftmost value the client wrote.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:read: 200 + ETag "v7"later If-None-Match "v7"304write: If-Match "v7"compare in the write's transaction200 + "v8", or 412

Recall

Prompt Answer
If-Match stale gives? If-None-Match match on GET gives? 412; 304.
Which comparison does each use? If-Match strong (MUST); If-None-Match weak (MUST).
Which X-Forwarded-For entry can you trust? Only what your own proxies added, counted from the right.

The idea

Two support agents open ticket 8f2 at version "v7". Agent A saves a note, and agent B saves a status 30 seconds later from the same stale copy. Both get 200, and A's note is gone. No log records it, because nothing failed.

Send If-Match: "v7" on the writes. A's save makes it "v8". B's still names "v7", so the origin answers 412. B re-reads it.

It works only if the compare and the write are atomic. Compare in the handler and write later, and you've rebuilt the race.

The trade: a precondition turns a silent lost update into a visible 412, and you pay for a validator on every resource and a client that can rebase.

How it works

The nine, by the job they do and who acts on them.

Job Header Direction Who acts on it
Negotiation Content-Type, Accept both, request origin; 406, 415 when they fail
Auth Authorization request gateway, origin; shared caches won't reuse the response without permission
Caching Cache-Control both every cache (owner)
Validators ETag, If-None-Match response, request cache and origin; 304
Concurrency If-Match request origin only; 412
Retry Retry-After response client (owner); seconds or an HTTP-date
Correlation X-Request-ID, traceparent both edge sets, every hop logs (tracing)
Client address X-Forwarded-For, Forwarded request proxies append, the app reads

When several conditions arrive, RFC 9110 §13.2.2 fixes the order, which is how a resume and a lost-update guard coexist on one request:

If-Unmodified-Since stands in for If-Match and If-Modified-Since is ignored when If-None-Match is present; both date forms are second-resolution, so ETags win on anything contended.

Rule What actually happens
Weak tags W/"7" means equivalent, not identical. If-None-Match accepts it; If-Match can never match it.
Forwarded chain Each proxy appends the peer it saw, so the right end is yours and the left end is the client's word.
The middle stays out A proxy that can't act as a cache MUST forward conditional fields and MUST NOT evaluate them (§13.2.1).

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): RFC 9110 consolidates all of these except X-Forwarded-For, a de-facto field; Forwarded (RFC 7239) standardised it in 2014 and coexists with it.
  • Changed in RFC 9110 (Jun 2022): conditional requests moved from RFC 7232 into §13, with the same comparison rules.
  • What's next and what won't change: traceparent keeps replacing bespoke request ids. A client-writable field stays untrustworthy however it's named.

On the wire

Captured 1 Nov 2026 from our own http.server handler and proxy on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15.0, curl 8.7.1), trimmed. The ETag compare is our code, written to the RFC's rules.

PUT /orders/8f2   (no If-Match)
HTTP/1.1 428 Precondition Required      # this server demands one

PUT /orders/8f2   If-Match: W/"v7"
HTTP/1.1 412 Precondition Failed        # weak tag: strong compare fails

PUT /orders/8f2   If-Match: "v7"   {"status":"shipped"}
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "v8"

PUT /orders/8f2   If-Match: "v7"   {"status":"cancelled"}
HTTP/1.1 412 Precondition Failed        # the later GET shows "shipped", still v8
ETag: "v8"

Break it: the client writes the left end of the chain.

curl $P/xff                                   # our proxy appends the peer
curl -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 6.6.6.6' $P/xff     # the client claims an address first
# look for: the leftmost entry the app sees
# naive belief predicts: the proxy replaces it, so 6.6.6.6 never arrives

Run: 127.0.0.1, then 6.6.6.6, 127.0.0.1. A limiter on the leftmost value keys on what the caller typed.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -i a PUT with a stale If-Match shows 412 and an unchanged resource; curl -H 'X-Forwarded-For: …' through your edge shows what the app receives.
  • In production: 412 rate per route (zero on a contended resource means clients don't send it); per request, the share carrying your request id; rate-limit keys sharing a leftmost address.
  • Bounded by: a lost update → If-Match compared inside the write's transaction, with 428 when absent; a spoofed address → the trusted-proxy count, read from the right.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Most of HTTP's real behaviour lives in headers: negotiation, auth, caching, concurrency, retry hints, correlation. The two I'd call out: If-Match is the only thing that stops two different writers overwriting each other, since idempotency keys only stop the same write twice. And X-Forwarded-For is a list the client starts, so only entries your own proxies added are trustworthy.

Q · Mechanism — Why strong comparison for If-Match and weak for If-None-Match? They protect different things. If-None-Match asks whether a stored copy is still good enough to reuse, and a weak tag saying "semantically equivalent" answers that. If-Match guards a write, so the RFC requires strong comparison: anything less could allow a change based on bytes that differ. The strong-comparison table shows even W/"1" against W/"1" doesn't match. So a server that only emits weak tags can't support If-Match, and every PUT gets 412.

Q · Trade-off — When is last-write-wins acceptable? When contention is rare and a lost field is an annoyance. Adopt preconditions when a resource is genuinely shared, or when a lost value is a compliance problem, and use 428 once clients have migrated, because 412 only helps those that opted in. The cost is a validator per resource and a real conflict flow in the UI, where a blind retry just reintroduces the overwrite.

Compare

ETag + If-Match Last-Modified + If-Unmodified-Since Version field in the body
Resolution exact one second exact
Failure answer 412 412 409, by convention
When you'd pick it contended resources static files a body-only protocol

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Date validator resolution 1 second HTTP-date format spec: RFC 9110 §5.6.7
X-Forwarded-For limit on ALB 30 addresses beyond it, 463 default (as of Nov 2026): ALB docs
Stale If-Match, write applied 0 second writer refused measured: curl 8.7.1, 1 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: If-Match vs If-None-Match
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both take an ETag, and both are "conditional".
    ↳ Difference: If-None-Match on a read saves bytes with 304, with weak comparison. If-Match on a write stops a lost update with 412, with strong comparison.
    ↳ Think instead: None-Match saves bytes; Match saves data.
  • "X-Forwarded-For is the client's IP"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's what frameworks expose as the remote address.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: MDN warns that any part not added by a trusted proxy may be spoofed, and that no part is trustworthy if the server is reachable directly.
    ↳ Think instead: count trusted proxies from the right, and block direct access to the origin.
  • Don't compare the ETag outside the write's transaction.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a read, an if, then an UPDATE looks correct and passes every test.
    ↳ What goes wrong: two requests pass the check together and both write, so the guard fails only under the race it exists for.
    ↳ Do instead: UPDATE … WHERE version = ?, and map zero rows to 412.
  • Don't send the same Retry-After to everyone.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a constant is simple, and it's what a gateway config offers.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every rejected client returns at the same instant, so the limit creates the next spike.
    ↳ Do instead: compute it per caller, and let clients add jitter.
  • Shelf life: the conditional rules are durable. Provider limits on forwarded headers change.

Connections

Path:choosing the right codeheadersHTTP caching
  • Used by REST: conditional reads and writes, shown in use.
  • Owned elsewhere: HTTP caching owns Cache-Control; rate limiting owns the server side of Retry-After.
  • Composes with idempotency keys: duplicates and overwrites need both.
  • Contrasts with distributed tracing: traceparent generalises the request id.

notes.title: HTTP Caching
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9111: HTTP Caching · 📜 RFC 5861: stale content extensions · 📜 RFC 8246: immutable · MDN: Cache-Control

TL;DR

Caching runs on two clocks. While a response is fresh, a cache answers with no trip to the origin. Once stale, it asks with If-None-Match and gets 304 or a new 200. Fresh saves the round trip; 304 saves only the bytes. Everything else decides who may store it, and Vary decides whose copy it is.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:requestkey: URI + Varystored?originfresh?serve, no tripIf-None-Match304, reuse, or 200, replace

Recall

Prompt Answer
no-cache vs no-store? no-cache: store, revalidate before reuse. no-store: don't store.
Which directives open a shared cache to Authorization responses? public, s-maxage, must-revalidate (RFC 9111 §3.5).
What does Vary: * do? Always fails to match, so nothing is reused unvalidated.

The idea

Four worked decisions, situation → checks → answer → defence:

  • A hashed bundle, app.3f9c.js. Per-user? no. Can the URL change on every build? yes. Answer: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. Defence: a new build makes a new URL, so nothing needs invalidating.
  • The HTML that names that bundle. Same URL each deploy? yes. Answer: no-cache with an ETag. Defence: every load asks, and a 304 costs one round trip, so a deploy shows at once.
  • GET /me. Per-user? yes. Answer: private, no-cache with an ETag. Defence: no shared cache may store it, and the browser gets cheap revalidation.
  • A public price list that may be a minute old. Staleness acceptable? yes. Answer: s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=30. Defence: s-maxage limits the CDN, and users don't wait on the background refresh.

The trade: a longer lifetime buys origin load and latency, and you pay in staleness you can't recall, so choose by what a wrong answer costs, not by what's easy to configure.

How it works

A shared cache between client and origin, through one object's life. ① costs the origin, ② costs nobody, ③ costs a round trip and no body.

The table to recall; each cache in the path runs this independently, and a directive binds only the caches it names.

Directive or header Binds Effect Use when
max-age=N all caches fresh for N seconds a known lifetime
s-maxage=N shared overrides max-age, adds proxy-revalidate CDN longer than browsers
no-cache all store, validate before reuse content that may change
no-store all don't store secrets, statements
private shared a shared cache MUST NOT store it per-user responses
public shared may store even with Authorization shared assets
must-revalidate all never reuse stale; 504 if disconnected correctness beats availability
immutable clients don't revalidate while fresh hashed URLs
stale-while-revalidate=N all reuse stale, refresh behind it hide refresh latency
stale-if-error=N all reuse stale on 500–504 outage cover
Vary all request fields join the key Accept-Encoding, Origin

With no directive, a cache may guess: heuristic freshness is common for heuristically cacheable codes, and RFC 9111 §4.2.2 suggests about 10% of the time since Last-Modified. So a missing header doesn't mean "not cached".

Which policy for this response? Each question removes a family, and the default leaf is cheap revalidation:

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): RFC 9111 is the base; immutable is in Firefox and Safari but not Chrome, by MDN's data.
  • Changed in RFC 9111 (Jun 2022): it obsoletes RFC 7234, renames "cacheable by default" to "heuristically cacheable" and drops the Warning field.
  • What's next and what won't change: CDN-Cache-Control (RFC 9213) and Cache-Status (RFC 9211) separate CDN policy and expose hits. The two clocks stay.

On the wire

Conditional GET to 304, captured 1 Nov 2026 from our own http.server handler on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15.0, curl 8.7.1), trimmed:

GET /orders/8f2
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "v7"
Cache-Control: private, max-age=0, must-revalidate
Content-Length: 33
{"id": "8f2", "status": "packed"}

GET /orders/8f2   If-None-Match: "v7"
HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified                 # keeps ETag and Cache-Control, no body
ETag: "v7"
Cache-Control: private, max-age=0, must-revalidate

GET /orders/8f2   If-None-Match: "v6"     # a version the server no longer has
HTTP/1.1 200 OK                           # the full body again
ETag: "v7"

Measure it

  • See it: Age on a response proves a cache served it; curl -i with If-None-Match shows 304 and no body; Cache-Status shows hits where a CDN sends it.
  • In production: per route, hit ratio and 304 share; origin requests per user request; a hit ratio falling after a Vary change points at key fragmentation.
  • Bounded by: one user's data served to another → private or no-store, Vary on what changes the body; a stale deploy → hashed URLs; a stampede at expiry → cascading failures.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Two clocks. While a response is fresh, any cache answers with no origin trip. When stale, it revalidates with an ETag and gets a 304 or a new body. The savings differ: fresh saves the round trip, 304 only the bytes. So max-age beats validators for small JSON. The worst failure isn't staleness, it's a shared cache serving one user's response to another, which private and Vary prevent.

Q · Mechanism — What decides whether a cache may reuse a stored response? Three checks. The key: URI and method match, and every field named by Vary matches the stored request, where Vary: * always fails. Permission: nothing like no-cache requires asking first. Freshness: age below lifetime, from s-maxage, max-age, Expires or a heuristic, in that order. If all pass, it serves with Age set. If only freshness fails, it validates, and 304 refreshes the stored headers. A cache that's disconnected may serve stale unless must-revalidate forbids it, when it answers 504.

Q · Trade-off — Short TTLs or versioned URLs when deploys must show within a minute? Versioned URLs, because invalidation is a naming problem before it's a TTL problem. Hash into the filename, serve immutable with a year's max-age, and the HTML, on no-cache, picks up the new name for one 304. No single TTL gives both an instant deploy and a high hit rate. It flips when you don't control the URL, as with API responses and third-party embeds: use a short s-maxage with stale-while-revalidate, and keep purges for emergencies.

Compare

Fresh hit 304 Full 200 When you'd pick it
Round trips to the origin 0 1 1
Body bytes 0 0 full
Pick a tolerable lifetime large bodies, changing rarely content changed

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Heuristic freshness about 10% of the interval since Last-Modified "a typical setting" spec: RFC 9111 §4.2.2
must-revalidate, disconnected 504 SHOULD be that code spec: RFC 9111 §5.2.2.2
CloudFront default TTL 24 hours if you don't use a cache policy default (as of Nov 2026): CloudFront docs
Body on 304 in our capture 0 of 33 bytes one round trip still paid measured: curl 8.7.1, 1 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "no-cache means don't cache"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the name says exactly that.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it stores the body and forbids reuse without validation, so it's usually a cheap 304. no-store is the one that forbids storing.
    ↳ Think instead: no-cache is "always ask"; no-store is "never keep".
  • "no-store keeps it private"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the strongest directive there is.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: RFC 9111 says it "is not a reliable or sufficient mechanism for ensuring privacy": a malicious cache may ignore it, and only well-behaved ones obey.
    ↳ Think instead: it's a request to honest caches. TLS and authorisation protect the data.
  • Not the same: private vs no-store
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are the answer to "don't let the CDN have it".
    ↳ Difference: private lets the browser store it, while no-store stops every cache, and that costs a full reload.
    ↳ Think instead: per-user is private; secret is no-store.
  • "My CDN follows the origin's Cache-Control"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the header looks like a command.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: CloudFront with a minimum TTL above 0 caches even no-store responses for that TTL, and Set-Cookie changes behaviour by product.
    ↳ Think instead: read each cache's rules, and verify with Age.
  • Don't reach for CDN purge first.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it sounds exact: change something, purge it.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a purge is a distributed operation you must trigger and trust for every change, and variants can be missed.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: hashed URLs for assets, and short lifetimes elsewhere.
  • Shelf life: the RFC model is durable. CDN defaults, and browser support for immutable, move.

Connections

Path:headersHTTP cachingcontent negotiation and rangescookies
  • Builds on safe, idempotent, cacheable: which methods can be stored at all.
  • Used by CDN and edge: this model across PoPs, with key design and purge.
  • Composes with CORS: Vary: Origin is a caching rule.
  • Measured by latency vs bandwidth: why fresh hits and 304s aren't equal.
  • Drilled in where to put the cache.

notes.title: Cookies and Cookie Attributes
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 6265: HTTP State Management · 📜 draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis · MDN: Set-Cookie · MDN: Using HTTP cookies

TL;DR

The server sets a cookie, and the browser attaches it to every matching request by itself. That one behaviour gives you effortless sessions and also gives you CSRF. Every attribute is a rule the browser checks before sending, so a failed check arrives at your server as a missing cookie, with no explanation.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:Set-Cookiebrowser stores itnext requesthost and path match?Secure allows it?SameSite allows it?Cookie: attachedserver resolves the session

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does HttpOnly actually stop? document.cookie reads. Injected script can still send requests that carry it.
__Host- requires what? Secure, set from HTTPS, Path=/, and no Domain.
Who enforces SameSite? The browser. curl and your server never apply it.

The idea

A user is signed in to bank.example, then opens evil.example. That page auto-submits a form to bank.example/transfer. The browser attaches the session cookie, because attaching is its job, and the server sees a valid session. The attacker never read the cookie. They only caused it to be sent. That's CSRF, and a bearer token in an Authorization header can't suffer it, because nothing attaches a header by itself.

So cookies grew rules. SameSite=Lax keeps the cookie off that cross-site POST. HttpOnly keeps it out of script. Secure keeps it off plain HTTP. __Host- pins it to one host.

The trade: a cookie gives you automatic, script-proof credentials, and you pay by defending a request the browser sends for you.

How it works

Every question below is asked by the browser, before the request leaves, and your server sees only the result.

A session that "randomly" gives 401 is usually a red branch here, so debug in the browser's request view, not the server log.

Rule What actually happens
HttpOnly Hidden from document.cookie. Still sent on every matching request.
SameSite Strict never crosses sites. Lax crosses only on top-level navigation with a safe method. None always crosses, and needs Secure.
Domain Omit it and the cookie is host-only. Set it and every subdomain receives it, so it only ever widens.
Prefixes __Secure- needs Secure. __Host- adds Path=/ and no Domain. __Http- and __Host-Http- also need HttpOnly.
The middle A shared cache must not store a personalised response (HTTP caching). An L7 balancer may set its own stickiness cookie.

Evolution

  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established, Nov 2026. RFC 6265 dates from 2011 and is still the published standard, and every browser ships cookies.
  • Changed in 6265bis: SameSite and the prefixes live in this revision, not in RFC 6265. It's draft 22 and still not an RFC as of Nov 2026, so cite MDN for browser behaviour.
  • What's next and what won't change: default-Lax varies by browser, and partitioned cookies (Partitioned, CHIPS) answer third-party use. Automatic attachment stays, and so does the need to defend it.

On the wire

Captured 1 Nov 2026 from our own http.server handler on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15.0, curl 8.7.1). curl -c is the jar, and the #HttpOnly_ marker is curl's own.

GET /login
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=abc123; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/
Set-Cookie: plain=1; Path=/

GET /me                 # curl -b jar
Cookie: __Host-sid=abc123; plain=1      # HttpOnly hides it from script, not the wire

Break it: does SameSite stop the request?

curl -s -b jar -H 'Origin: https://evil.example' \
     -H 'Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site' http://127.0.0.1:8077/me
# look for: the Cookie header the server echoes back
# naive belief predicts: SameSite=Lax keeps the cookie off a cross-site request

Run: the server echoed __Host-sid=abc123; plain=1. SameSite is the browser's rule, and curl isn't a browser, so a server that trusts it has defended only against browsers.

Measure it

  • See it: the browser's Network panel shows cookies with a reason when filtered out; correct is a sent cookie carrying every attribute you intended.
  • In production: per-request 401 rate by user agent and by origin. A jump for one browser after a release usually means a SameSite or Secure change.
  • Bounded by: session theft or forged writes → __Host- with HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, short server-side sessions you can revoke, plus an origin check or CSRF token on state-changing methods.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A cookie is state the browser attaches automatically to matching requests. That's why sessions are easy, and why CSRF exists: another site can cause a request that carries your session without reading it. HttpOnly, SameSite and __Host- shrink the risk. I default to an HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, __Host- session for a browser app, and tokens for clients with no cookie jar.

Q · Mechanism — What does each attribute change, and which are security controls? HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite and the prefixes are controls: they limit where the value can be read or sent. Domain, Path, Max-Age and Expires set scope and lifetime. Path isn't isolation, because same-origin script can load that path. Domain=example.com shares the cookie with every subdomain, including a forgotten one pointing at a decommissioned vendor. All of it is enforced by the browser, before sending, so nothing server-side confirms it happened.

Q · Trade-off — Single-page app and your API: HttpOnly session cookie, or a bearer token? The two attacks aren't symmetric. XSS against localStorage copies a token the attacker replays elsewhere until it expires. CSRF against a cookie makes blind requests, and Lax already blocks the cross-site POST. So I default to the cookie, on the same site. It flips for mobile, CLI and server callers, which have no jar, and for an API on another site, where SameSite=None gives up the protection. Then use a short-lived token, with the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie.

Compare

HttpOnly cookie Token in localStorage Token in memory When you'd pick it
Sent automatically yes no no cookie for a browser session
CSRF exposure yes, SameSite helps none none token across sites
Script can read it no yes yes, while the tab lives memory for a strict SPA
Survives reload yes yes no
Works without a browser poorly yes yes token for mobile and services

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Size a browser should support at least 4,096 bytes per cookie so hold an id, not state spec: RFC 6265 §6.1
Cookies per domain at least 50 a floor, not a limit spec: RFC 6265 §6.1
Default-Lax POST grace 2 minutes only when Lax was applied by default default (as of Nov 2026): MDN

Pitfalls

  • "HttpOnly protects against XSS"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the attribute always listed next to XSS.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it stops one step, reading the value. Injected script still runs in your origin and sends requests, and the browser attaches the cookie.
    ↳ Think instead: it limits theft to the live session. Stopping XSS is a separate job.
  • Not the same: same-site vs same-origin
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both sound like "my own site".
    ↳ Difference: app.example.com and api.example.com share a site but not an origin, so SameSite lets the cookie through while CORS still applies.
    ↳ Think instead: SameSite compares registrable domains; CORS compares scheme, host and port.
  • "SameSite alone finishes CSRF"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: Lax blocks the classic form post.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a sibling subdomain counts as same-site, the default varies by browser, and a cross-site top-level GET still carries it, so an unsafe GET stays exposed.
    ↳ Think instead: SameSite is one layer. Keep safe methods safe, and check origin on writes.
  • Don't widen Domain for convenience.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one login across every subdomain with a single attribute.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every subdomain can read it, so one taken-over host holds the session.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: host-only __Host- cookies, and a real login redirect between hosts.
  • Shelf life: 6265bis may publish, and default-Lax, third-party cookie policy and the new prefixes vary by browser. Re-check against MDN.

Connections

Path:HTTP cachingcookiesCORSidempotency keys
  • Builds on safe, idempotent, cacheable: Lax keys off the safe-method distinction.
  • Composes with CORS: credentialed requests need both sets of rules to pass.
  • Used by sticky sessions: an L7 balancer can pin clients with its own cookie.
  • Bounded by choosing the right code: a missing cookie surfaces as 401, not as an error naming it.
  • Decided in REST: statelessness pushes session state out of the server's memory.

notes.title: CORS and Preflight Requests
notes.html:
References

📜 Fetch Standard: CORS protocol · MDN: CORS · MDN: Access-Control-Max-Age · MDN: Access-Control-Allow-Headers

TL;DR

CORS is how a server tells the browser that script from another origin may read its response. The server only advertises; the browser enforces, so curl and Postman never see the problem. A simple request is sent and only its response is withheld. Anything else asks first with an OPTIONS preflight. CORS relaxes the same-origin policy. It protects nothing on your server.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:fetch()simple?send, then check Allow-Originread or withhold
fetch()OPTIONS preflightallowed?real requestnetwork error, nothing sent

Recall

Prompt Answer
Three common preflight triggers? Method beyond GET/HEAD/POST, JSON Content-Type, any non-safelisted header.
What does Allow-Credentials: true forbid? * in Allow-Origin, -Headers, -Methods and Expose-Headers.
What is the preflight cache keyed on? Origin, URL, credentials, and method or header. So each URL pays.

The idea

Your app at https://app.example.com calls https://api.example.com/orders with JSON. It works in Postman and fails in the browser, and the access log shows an OPTIONS with no POST after it.

Postman has no same-origin policy to relax. The browser does: script from one origin can't read another origin's response unless that server says so. JSON is a body an old HTML form couldn't send, so the browser asks permission first, and your server didn't answer in a way it accepts.

The rule exists to protect servers built before CORS. A request shape a form could already send gets no preflight, so it adds no new risk. Anything new must be allowed in advance.

The trade: cross-origin reads without opening every origin, and you pay a round trip per uncached URL, plus one exact allowlist to maintain.

How it works

The preflight is a separate round trip with no credentials, and the real request follows only if it passes.

So a server log with 200 can sit beside a console error.

Rule What actually happens
Simple GET, HEAD or POST, safelisted headers, and Content-Type of form, multipart or text/plain. Sent straight away.
Preflight must pass An ok (2xx) status and matching headers. A 401 from auth middleware fails it, because preflights carry no credentials.
Credentials Needs Allow-Credentials: true and explicit values. Set-Cookie is ignored if Allow-Origin is *.
Authorization Never covered by Allow-Headers: *, so name it.
The middle A gateway may answer OPTIONS itself, a CDN needs Vary: Origin when you echo origins, and limiters count preflights.

Evolution

  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established, Nov 2026. The W3C spec was absorbed by the Fetch Standard, which browsers implement.
  • Changed by browser limits: Chromium caps Max-Age at 2 hours from v76; it was 10 minutes before. Firefox allows 24 hours. Without the header it's 5 seconds.
  • What's next and what won't change: browsers keep adding limits on private-network requests. The server advertises and the browser enforces.

On the wire

Captured 1 Nov 2026 from our own http.server handler on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15.0, curl 8.7.1); the policy is our code. curl plays the browser's preflight here, by hand.

OPTIONS /x
Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: PUT, POST
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization
Access-Control-Max-Age: 7200
Vary: Origin                    # the same URL answers differently per Origin

OPTIONS /x
Origin: https://evil.example    # not on the list: 204, no Allow-Origin

Break it: does a CORS failure mean the server did nothing?

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8077/delete-account \
     -H 'Origin: https://evil.example' -H 'Content-Type: text/plain' -d x
