# look for: whether the side effect ran with no Allow-Origin in the response
# naive belief predicts: the unlisted origin is refused, so the counter stays 0

Run twice: executed, count=1, then count=2, each a 200 with no Allow-Origin. A browser would send this simple shape too, and only hide the answer.

Measure it

  • See it: the Network panel shows the OPTIONS row before the real one; correct is a 2xx with the expected headers, and no repeat within Max-Age.
  • In production: per-route share of OPTIONS in request logs, and browser errors from real-user monitoring. OPTIONS near 50% on a hot route means the cache isn't helping.
  • Bounded by: an extra round trip per URL and a cross-origin read leak → same-origin routing, a stable URL shape, Max-Age, and an exact allowlist with Vary: Origin. Real access control stays in auth.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: CORS lets a server tell the browser which other origins may read its responses. Only the browser enforces it, so Postman works while the browser fails. Simple requests are sent and the response withheld. JSON, PUT or a custom header trigger an OPTIONS preflight first. It isn't a server-side control: authentication does that job, and CORS only relaxes the same-origin policy.

Q · Mechanism — What exactly does the preflight exchange, and what does it cost? It's an OPTIONS with Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method and -Headers, and no credentials. The server replies with the allowed origin, methods and headers and an optional Max-Age, and it must be a 2xx. Then the real request goes. The browser caches per origin, URL and credentials mode, with a method or header in each entry, so /orders/1 and /orders/2 are separate. Path parameters make a poor cache key, and one RTT is paid per URL per lifetime.

Q · Trade-off — A team wants Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on an API. Allow it? Yes for a public, credential-free, read-only endpoint, where it's the simplest honest answer. Otherwise no. With cookies it doesn't even work, because the browser rejects * on credentialed requests. Use an exact allowlist, echo the match, and send Vary: Origin, or a CDN will serve one origin's answer to another and fail for some users only. The better default is often none of this: route /api on the same origin, and every preflight disappears.

Compare

Simple Preflighted Credentialed When you'd pick it
Extra round trip no yes, per URL if also preflighted keep hot reads simple
Allow-Origin: * legal yes yes no public data only
Sent if the policy says no yes no depends on preflight
Script can read the answer if origin matches if origin matches also needs Allow-Credentials

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Max-Age when absent 5 s or invalid spec: Fetch §4.8
Max-Age cap, Chromium 7,200 s 600 s before v76 default (as of Nov 2026): MDN
Max-Age cap, Firefox 86,400 s default (as of Nov 2026): MDN
Preflight cost 1 RTT per URL per lifetime on top of the request derived

Pitfalls

  • "A CORS error means the request never reached my server"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the console says "blocked".
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a simple request ran to completion, as the run above shows. Only the response was hidden from script. A failed preflight is the one case that stops the real request.
    ↳ Think instead: CORS blocks reading, not sending. Protect side effects with auth and a CSRF defence.
  • Not the same: 401 on preflight vs 401 on the request
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both look like an auth failure.
    ↳ Difference: a preflight carries no credentials, so auth middleware that covers OPTIONS rejects every caller, even signed-in ones.
    ↳ Think instead: answer OPTIONS before auth runs, and then look at the real request.
  • Don't reflect Origin without an allowlist.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it clears the error for every environment with one line.
    ↳ What goes wrong: with Allow-Credentials: true, any page can read signed-in responses. A loose regex for example.com also matches example.com.attacker.net.
    ↳ Do instead: compare against exact origins.
  • Don't reach for CORS when one origin would do.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: separate app and API hosts look tidy.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a permanent preflight cost, plus a header matrix that breaks with each new environment.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: a path route to the API behind one origin.
  • Shelf life: the protocol is stable. Max-Age caps and private-network rules move by browser.

Connections

Path:cookiesCORSidempotency keysrate limiting
  • Builds on HTTP methods: OPTIONS, and the form-era GET and POST shape.
  • Composes with cookies: credentialed requests must satisfy both sets of rules.
  • Composes with HTTP caching: Vary: Origin is a caching rule, and missing it fails for some users.
  • Breaks when combined with rate limiting: preflights consume quota unless excluded.
  • Owned elsewhere: API gateway own where the policy is configured.

notes.title: Idempotency Keys

References

📜 Idempotency-Key header draft · 📜 RFC 9110 §9.2.2: Idempotent Methods · Stripe: Idempotent requests · MDN: HTTP request methods

TL;DR

A timeout on a POST leaves the client not knowing whether the charge happened. So the client mints one key per logical operation and resends it on every retry. The server's first act, before any side effect, is an atomic insert of that key. The winner does the work and stores the response, and a loser replays it. The insert is the lock.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:client mints keyPOST + keyatomic insertside effectstore response201
retry, same keyinsert conflictsfingerprint differs? 422still running? 409done? replay 201

Recall

Prompt Answer
One key per what? Per logical operation, reused on every retry, never per attempt.
Why is "check, then process" broken? Two concurrent retries both find nothing, and both charge.
What does the record hold? Scoped key, state, fingerprint, response status and body, expiry.
Draft's codes: missing, reused, in flight? 400, 422, 409.
How long must the record live? Longer than the client's whole retry window.
Draw by hand: three attempts of one charge Insert wins and runs; second conflicts, 409; third conflicts, replays stored 201.

The idea

A client posts a $49.99 charge. The processor charges the card, but the response dies on the way back, and the client's timeout fires. It can't tell "never arrived" from "done, reply lost". Retrying may charge twice, and not retrying may lose the sale. POST promises nothing here, so the method can't help.

Add a key the client generated before the first attempt. The retry arrives with the same key, the server recognises the operation, and it returns the original 201 with the original charge id. Duplicate arrivals stay possible, and they stop mattering: delivery is still at-least-once, and the effect happens once.

Recognition is the easy half. It also has to be mutual exclusion, because retries arrive while the first attempt is still running.

The trade: a write path safe to retry, and you pay for a store on every write, an expiry policy, and a new tier-0 dependency.

How it works

Three attempts of one operation. The constraint decides who works, not application code.

Attempt ② never reaches the side effect, because the database refused it. Returning 409 pushes the wait onto the client's backoff and frees a server thread.

Rule What actually happens
Insert first INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING before any side effect. exists() then write reopens the race, however small.
Scope Unique on tenant, endpoint and key. Without tenant, one customer can receive another's response.
Fingerprint Hash the meaningful body, excluding timestamps. Same key with a different body is rejected, never replayed.
Replay Return the stored status and body, because the client needs the id it never received.
The middle The key lets a client, SDK or gateway retry a POST. A proxy still must not retry it automatically unless it knows. 
live rows = write rate × retention        ← every key stays until it expires
          = 10,000/s × 86,400 s = 864M    ← at a 24-hour retention
so: partition by time, drop whole tables  ← a DELETE scan can't keep up cleanly

Evolution

Lineage:2015 Stripe's Idempotency-Key in practicepayments APIs copy itIETF httpapi draft2026 draft 08
  • Maturity today: 🟡 Maturing, Nov 2026. The pattern is settled, while the header's spec is an active draft and not an RFC.
  • Changed in the draft: the value is a structured-field string, so it's quoted ("k1"). Fingerprints are optional, and a resource should publish its expiry policy.
  • What's next and what won't change: Stripe's API v2 retries failed work to completion rather than replaying a stored failure. The insert before the side effect won't change.

On the wire

Captured 1 Nov 2026 from our own http.server handler on 127.0.0.1, with SQLite 3.54.1 as the store (Python 3.15.0, curl 8.7.1). The statuses are our code, following the draft's recommendations.

POST /charges                                  # no key
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request

POST /charges  Idempotency-Key: "k1"  {"amount":4999}   # ① still running
POST /charges  Idempotency-Key: "k1"  {"amount":4999}   # ② sent 0.1 s later
HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict
Retry-After: 1

HTTP/1.1 201 Created        # ① finishes
{"id": "ch_1"}

POST /charges  Idempotency-Key: "k1"  {"amount":4999}   # ③
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
{"id": "ch_1"}              # replayed, one charge recorded

POST /charges  Idempotency-Key: "k1"  {"amount":9999}
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content

Break it: is checking first good enough?

# 8 threads release from a barrier against one SQLite file; 10 ms models the call
def check_then_act(c):
    if c.execute("select 1 from idem where key='k'").fetchone() is None:
        time.sleep(0.01)
        c.execute("insert or ignore into idem values('k')")
        c.execute("insert into charges(key) values('k')")
def insert_first(c):
    if c.execute("insert into idem values('k') on conflict do nothing").rowcount == 1:
        time.sleep(0.01); c.execute("insert into charges(key) values('k')")
# look for: rows in charges after 8 concurrent attempts
# naive belief predicts: 1 in both, since the check sees the key

Run five times each on Python 3.15.0 and SQLite 3.54.1: check_then_act recorded 8 charges every time, and insert_first recorded 1 every time. The barrier and the sleep make the race easy to hit, and the point is that the second version has no window at all.

Measure it

  • See it: send the same key twice with curl -i; correct is one row in the side-effect table and the same id in both responses.
  • In production: per-request conflict rate, 409 rate, and fingerprint mismatches. A rising 409 rate means client timeouts sit below server p99, and any mismatch means a client bug.
  • Bounded by: a duplicate side effect → the unique constraint, in the same transaction as the write where possible, and a retention longer than the retry window.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A timeout on a POST can't tell the client whether the work happened. So it sends one key per logical operation on every retry. The server inserts that key atomically before any side effect; the winner works and stores the response, a loser replays it. It's at-least-once delivery with one effect. Everything rests on that insert, not on a check.

Q · Mechanism — What does the server do when a keyed request arrives? It fingerprints the body and inserts the scoped key in state processing. Winning the insert means this request owns the operation, so it runs the side effect, then stores status and body. Losing means reading the row: a different fingerprint gets 422, processing gets 409, and complete gets the stored response replayed. Storing only "already done" isn't enough, since the client still needs the charge id it never received.

Q · Trade-off — The operation fails halfway. Release the key, or record the failure? Release it only when the failure provably came before any external call, such as validation or quota. Otherwise a retry may charge again. Record it when you can't prove that: safe, but the client is stuck with that failure until expiry and must mint a new key. Stripe's API v1 takes the second path once execution begins, saving even a 500, while it doesn't save validation failures or concurrency conflicts, so those can be retried.

Q · Failure — The key store slows down and write p99 climbs. What's happening? The store's connection pool or write capacity is running out, and every write waits on it twice: insert, then completion. Availability is now the product of both systems, so a less available store caps the API. Confirm with store p99 and pool wait per write. For money, fail closed with 503 and Retry-After: a pause beats a duplicate charge. For a billed LLM generation, you might fail open, because a duplicate costs tokens rather than trust.

Q · Design — Where does the key store live in a payments service? The binding constraint is that the key and the business write must commit together. So it's a table beside charges in the same database, not a separate Redis: a key set just before a crash claims work that never happened. ClientAPIinsert plus charge in one transaction. An external processor can't join that transaction, so pass your key on to it too, then reconcile. Shard on the key, partition by time. I'd watch mismatches first. See the flash sale design and service communication.

Compare

Approach Identity comes from Needs a store When you'd pick it
PUT /orders/{client-uuid} client no the client can own the id
Natural key + constraint the domain reuses your table it already has identity: invoice, delivery id
Idempotency-Key header client, for dedup only yes server-assigned ids and POST
GET before retry nobody no a server you can't change; racy

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Missing, reused, in flight 400, 422, 409 SHOULD spec: draft 08 §2.7
Stripe key length up to 255 characters V4 UUIDs suggested default (as of Nov 2026): Stripe docs
Stripe v1 retention prunable once at least 24 hours old a reused key after that is a new request default (as of Nov 2026): Stripe docs
Store round trips per write 2 insert, then completion derived
Live rows 864M 10,000 writes/s, 24 hours derived

Pitfalls

  • "Idempotency keys give you exactly-once delivery"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the customer sees one charge.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: duplicates still arrive, because no transport can prevent that. The server makes them harmless, so the guarantee lives in the write path.
    ↳ Think instead: at-least-once delivery, one effect. Exactly-once owns the wider argument.
  • "Redis SETNX with a TTL is enough"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's atomic, fast, and has expiry built in.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it isn't in your business transaction. If the process dies after the set, the key claims an operation that never committed.
    ↳ Think instead: same transaction as the write, or budget for a reconciliation job.
  • Not the same: idempotency key vs If-Match
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both make retried writes "safe".
    ↳ Difference: a key stops the same write landing twice; a precondition stops two different writes overwriting each other.
    ↳ Think instead: duplicates need a key; ordering needs a version.
  • Don't mint the key inside the retry loop.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "a fresh UUID per request" is the usual habit.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every attempt looks new, so you have a plain POST wearing a header, invisible until a duplicate lands.
    ↳ Do instead: create it once with the operation, and persist it across restarts.
  • Don't let retention end before retries do.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: short expiry keeps the table small.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a late retry finds no record and runs again, hours after the first.
    ↳ Do instead: set retention above the longest retry, queue or replay window, and publish it.
  • Don't build a store when identity exists.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the pattern everyone copies from payments.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a parallel store and expiry job for a guarantee you already had.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: a unique constraint on your own table, or PUT to a client-chosen URI.
  • Shelf life: the draft may change status codes before it's an RFC, and Stripe's v2 behaviour differs from v1. The insert-first rule is durable.

Connections

Path:safe, idempotent, cacheableidempotency keystimeouts and retriesrate limiting
  • Builds on safe, idempotent, cacheable: why POST needs this and PUT doesn't.
  • Composes with headers: If-Match handles ordering, which keys don't.
  • Used by timeouts and retries: every retry of a write carries the same key.
  • Owned elsewhere: exactly-once owns dedup beyond HTTP, such as consumers and webhooks.
  • Bounded by choosing the right code: 409 and 422 must keep their distinct retry meanings.
  • Drilled in idempotent POST, idempotent endpoint.

notes.title: Timeouts, Retries & Exponential Backoff with Jitter
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9110 §10.2.3: Retry-After · AWS: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter · AWS: Exponential Backoff and Jitter · Google SRE: Handling Overload · MDN: Retry-After

TL;DR

Retries hide transient failures, and under load they turn a slow dependency into an outage. The client's contract has four parts: a timeout, retry only what can succeed later, back off, and add jitter. Backoff spreads retries over time, and jitter stops clients moving in lockstep. A budget then caps their total. A server's Retry-After beats your own guess.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:attempt ─timeout or 503transient?idempotent or keyed?budget left?Retry-After or random(0, min(cap, base·2ⁿ))sleepattempt, same key

Recall

Prompt Answer
The Full Jitter formula? random(0, min(cap, base × 2^n)): randomise the whole interval.
Why jitter at all? Without it, clients that failed together retry together.
Which failures do you retry? Connect errors, timeouts, 408, 429, 502, 503, 504.
Which do you never retry? 400, 401, 403, 404, 422: the same request fails identically.
Retry-After value forms? Delay in seconds, or an HTTP-date.
Draw by hand: the retry decision Transient? Idempotent or keyed? Budget left? Then wait, retry; otherwise fail.

The idea

A backend blips and returns 503 to 1,000 clients at once. Each waits a fixed 0.5 s and retries, so the backend takes all 1,000 again in the same instant. Doubling the wait doesn't help: they're still synchronised, and now the waves are further apart, with silence between them.

Randomise the wait, and those 1,000 retries spread across the window. Same requests, no wall. The backend gets a steady flow it can serve while it recovers.

That's the mechanical part. The judgement is deciding what deserves a retry at all. A 422 fails forever, so a retry only burns capacity. A POST without a key may charge twice. And a retry during an outage is extra load, at the worst moment.

The trade: a retry policy makes transient failures invisible, and you pay with a longer tail and extra load exactly when the dependency is weakest.

How it works

The checks run in this order, cheapest and most certain first, and each "no" fails fast.

Nothing retries until the question "could this work later?" has a yes, and that answer comes from the status code.

Rule What actually happens
Timeout first Nothing else can engage while you're still waiting. Keep connect short, and set the read timeout from a downstream percentile. Timeout hierarchy owns the chain.
Classify The status says retry or stop (choosing the right code). 500 is a per-API decision; AWS SDKs retry it.
Honour the server Retry-After on 429 or 503 beats a local guess. Add a little jitter, or callers told the same time return together.
One layer Retries multiply across layers: 3 attempts at 3 layers is 3³ = 27 calls. AWS's five-deep example reaches 243×. Retries done right owns budgets.
The middle A proxy or mesh retry counts as a layer. A gateway must not retry a POST it can't prove is safe.

Evolution

Lineage:1997 Retry-After in HTTP/1.12015 AWS publishes the jitter comparison2016 AWS SDK retry token bucket2026 AWS SDK update puts full jitter in the standard mode
  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established, Nov 2026. AWS SDKs, Envoy and gRPC all ship budgets or throttles as configuration.
  • What's next and what won't change: AWS's 2026 behaviour is opt-in until it becomes default. Providers keep adding their own hints, such as x-amz-retry-after. A retry remains extra load, whoever sends it.

On the wire

The loop, with the order of decisions above. Illustrative: it's a shape to copy, and budget is whatever token bucket your stack has.

RETRYABLE = {408, 429, 502, 503, 504}
BASE, CAP, MAX_ATTEMPTS = 0.05, 20.0, 3    # seconds; attempts includes the first

def call(send, key, budget):
    for n in range(MAX_ATTEMPTS):
        wait = None
        try:
            r = send(idempotency_key=key)  # SAME key on every attempt
            if r.status not in RETRYABLE:
                return r                   # includes 4xx: never retry those
            after = r.headers.get("Retry-After")
            wait = float(after) if after and after.isdigit() else None
        except (ConnectError, TimeoutError):
            pass                           # no response, so no hint
        if n == MAX_ATTEMPTS - 1 or not budget.allow():
            break                          # shed, don't pile on
        time.sleep(wait if wait is not None
                   else random.uniform(0, min(CAP, BASE * 2 ** n)))
    raise Exhausted(key)

Break it: is exponential backoff enough without jitter?

# 1,000 clients all fail at t=0; 4 attempts each; base 0.5 s, cap 20 s
for _ in range(1000):
    t = 0
    for n in range(4):
        d = min(20, .5 * 2**n)
        t += d if mode == "none" else random.uniform(0, d) if mode == "full" else d/2 + random.uniform(0, d/2)
        buckets[int(t * 10)] += 1          # requests per 100 ms
# look for: the busiest 100 ms bucket
# naive belief predicts: exponential spacing already spreads the load

Run with Python 3.15.0, seed 7. It's a client-side simulation, with no server behind it.

Strategy Peak per 100 ms Busy buckets Total requests
No jitter 1,000 4 4,000
Equal jitter 402 59 4,000
Full jitter 301 71 4,000

Exponential backoff alone left every wave at the full 1,000. Jitter cut the peak by about 70% with the same total, so it reshapes the load; it doesn't reduce it. Only a budget does that.

Measure it

  • See it: curl --retry 3 -v against a local 503 shows the attempts and the waits; correct is growing gaps and Retry-After honoured.
  • In production: per-dependency ratio of attempts to unique requests, near 1 when healthy, and in-flight calls per dependency. In-flight leads error rate.
  • Bounded by: retry amplification → one retrying layer, attempts capped at about 3, a retry budget, a circuit breaker for sustained failure.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Retries make transient failures invisible, and under load they multiply traffic on something already failing. So: a timeout shorter than the caller's budget, retry only failures that can succeed later, exponential backoff, and full jitter so clients don't return together. I honour Retry-After when the server sends it, retry at one layer, and cap volume with a budget. Writes carry an idempotency key.

Q · Mechanism — Why does randomising beat waiting longer? Waiting longer only moves a synchronised wave. Every client that failed together computes the same delay, so the server sees spikes and silence. Full jitter draws from the entire window, which turns each wave into a roughly constant rate. In our simulation of 1,000 clients, the peak per 100 ms fell from 1,000 to 301 with the same 4,000 requests. AWS calls the return on that complexity "huge". The AWS SDK's own formula is the same one, with a 20-second cap.

Q · Trade-off — When does adding retries lower availability? Retries help when failures are rare and independent, because a second attempt is nearly a fresh chance. They hurt when failures are correlated, because then every client retries against the same overloaded dependency. That's when availability matters most. A retried request also lengthens the tail by its own latency plus backoff. So I cap attempts per request and volume per client. Google's SRE book uses 3 attempts and a 10% retry ratio, which holds growth to about 1.1× in the general case.

Q · Failure — A dependency degrades to 5 s and your service falls over. What ran out? Threads and pooled connections ran out, not error budget. Callers block, the pool fills, and requests that never touch that dependency queue behind them. Timeouts then fire and retries add load, so the dependency can't recover, even after the original fault clears. Confirm with in-flight per dependency and pool wait. Fix in order: a short timeout, a separate pool per dependency, a breaker, then a budget. Cascading failures owns the full shape.

Q · Design — Design the policy for a service calling an LLM provider that sometimes returns 429. The binding constraint is that a retry costs a full generation in time and money, so "retry 3 times" is wrong. Separate the classes. 429 with Retry-After is a schedule: obey it. A connect error before any token is cheap to retry. A failure mid-stream isn't retryable without billing twice. Clientgateway, no retriesservice client, which owns retries, an idempotency key and a per-provider breaker with a fallback. Watch cost per successful completion. Provider timeouts and retries owns this path; see resilience patterns.

Compare

Strategy Sleep Behaviour When you'd pick it
Fixed delay base clients stay synchronised one client, a known wait
Exponential, no jitter min(cap, base × 2^n) spaced, still in lockstep never, for many clients
Equal jitter half fixed, half random avoids very short sleeps you need a minimum wait
Full jitter random(0, min(cap, base × 2^n)) spreads the whole window the default
Decorrelated jitter range grows from the last sleep keeps per-client state a library already gives it

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Amplification, 3 × 3 × 3 27× attempts per layer, three layers derived
AWS's five-deep example 243× 3 retries per layer spec: AWS Builders' Library
Peak, no jitter vs full 1,000 vs 301 per 100 ms 1,000 clients, base 0.5 s measured: Python 3.15.0, 1 Nov 2026
SRE retry limits 3 attempts, 10% ratio per request, per client spec: Google SRE book
AWS SDK default attempts 3, including the first standard mode default (as of Nov 2026): AWS SDK docs
AWS SDK base delay 50 ms transient, 1,000 ms throttling 20 s cap default (as of Nov 2026): AWS SDK docs, opt-in

Pitfalls

  • "Jitter is a micro-optimisation"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: backoff already "slows down", so randomness looks cosmetic.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: in the run above, backoff alone kept every wave at 1,000. Spacing doesn't help when everyone is spaced identically.
    ↳ Think instead: backoff sets how long; jitter stops everyone waiting the same long.
  • "More retries means higher availability"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's true when failures are independent.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: in a correlated failure they add load, and a system can stay down after the fault clears, because the backlog sustains the overload.
    ↳ Think instead: attempts raise availability only until they become the outage. Cap the volume.
  • Not the same: retry vs idempotency
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are said in the same sentence about safe writes.
    ↳ Difference: a retry policy decides when to send again; an idempotency key decides what a duplicate does.
    ↳ Think instead: the key makes a retry correct; backoff and budget make it safe.
  • Not the same: timeout vs deadline
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "how long I'll wait".
    ↳ Difference: a timeout is a fixed duration per hop, while a deadline is the remaining time, passed down, so it shrinks by itself.
    ↳ Think instead: set one budget at the edge and propagate it, as the hierarchy shows.
  • Don't retry at every layer.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: each team adds a retry to protect its own service.
    ↳ What goes wrong: browser, gateway and service multiply to 27 calls for one request.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: retry once, at the layer that knows whether the call is safe, and fail fast elsewhere.
  • Shelf life: the formula and the arithmetic are durable. SDK defaults change: AWS's 2026 behaviour is still opt-in.

Connections

Path:idempotency keystimeouts and retriesrate limitingtimeout hierarchy
  • Builds on safe, idempotent, cacheable: whether a retry is legal at all.
  • Composes with rate limiting: 429 and Retry-After are the server half of this contract.
  • Owned elsewhere: timeout hierarchy owns the chain; retries done right owns budgets.
  • Bounded by circuit breakers: retries handle transient faults, breakers handle sustained ones.
  • Used by provider timeouts and retries: this contract, when a retry is expensive.
  • Measured by triage playbooks: a retry storm has a recognisable shape.

notes.title: Rate Limiting and 429
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 6585 §4: 429 Too Many Requests · 📜 RateLimit header fields draft · MDN: Retry-After

TL;DR

A limiter decides from what a caller has already used, and the algorithm is really a burst policy: a token bucket allows saved-up bursts, a leaky bucket smooths them, and a fixed window admits twice the limit across a boundary. The contract matters as much as the counter: 429 plus Retry-After, so clients wait instead of hammering.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:requestkey: tenant or API keyrefill: elapsed × ratetoken?spend, serve429 + Retry-Afterclient waits, retries

Recall

Prompt Answer
Token bucket vs leaky bucket? Token allows bursts up to capacity; leaky enforces a constant outflow.
Fixed window's flaw? Twice the limit around a boundary: 200 admitted in 0.2 s at limit 100.
429 vs 503? 429 is this caller's rate. 503 is the server, for everyone.

The idea

You allow 100 requests a minute per key, with a counter per minute. A client sends 100 at 0:59.9 and 100 at 1:00.1. Each minute's counter is fine, and your database took 200 in 0.2 s. The limit protected a chart, not the downstream.

A token bucket closes that gap. Tokens refill continuously, so after spending 100 the client has almost none 0.2 s later, while an idle client can still burst. So the algorithm is really how much burst the thing behind it can take.

The trade: a limit protects a dependency and keeps callers fair, and you pay with a counter on every request, plus a new dependency if that counter is shared.

How it works

The bucket needs two numbers and no background job, because refill is computed on arrival.

tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsed × rate)   ← refill on arrival
allow  = tokens ≥ 1, then tokens -= 1             ← atomic with the read
Retry-After = ceil((1 − tokens) ÷ rate)           ← time until one token
Rule What actually happens
Key Tenant or API key first. IP alone lumps a whole NAT together, and an attacker rotates it.
Shared counter Per-node counters admit N × limit: 12 nodes admit 1,200 at limit 100, and autoscaling raises it silently.
Atomic Read, refill and spend are one step: a Lua script or a transaction. A plain read-then-write undercounts under load.
When the limiter fails Fail open for fairness limits. Fail closed for hard capacity. Alert either way.
The middle A gateway or edge usually enforces it, so your app logs nothing. X-Forwarded-For is only as trustworthy as your proxy. Preflights count unless excluded.

Evolution

  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established, Nov 2026. RFC 6585 defined 429 in 2012, and the algorithms are decades-old traffic-shaping ideas.
  • Changed in the RateLimit draft: two fields replace the X-RateLimit-* habit, RateLimit-Policy (q, w, pk) and RateLimit (r, t). t is relative seconds, which avoids clock skew. It's draft 11, not an RFC.
  • What's next and what won't change: provider limits are moving to token and spend budgets for AI traffic. 429 plus a wait stays the contract, and Retry-After beats the draft's window when both appear.

On the wire

Captured 1 Nov 2026 from our own http.server handler on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15.0, curl 8.7.1), a token bucket of capacity 3 refilling at 1 per second. The RateLimit field is our code, following draft 11.

GET /limited
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
RateLimit: "default";r=2;t=3

GET /limited
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
RateLimit: "default";r=1;t=3

GET /limited
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
RateLimit: "default";r=0;t=3

GET /limited
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 1                  # wait until one token has refilled

Break it: is a fixed window close enough?

# limit 100 per 60 s; 100 requests at t=59.9, 100 more at t=60.1
for t in [59.9]*100 + [60.1]*100:
    k = int(t // 60)
    if c.get(k, 0) < 100: c[k] = c.get(k, 0) + 1; ok += 1
# look for: how many were admitted in those 0.2 s
# naive belief predicts: about 100, because the limit is 100

Run: the fixed window admitted 200, a token bucket of capacity 100 admitted 100, and a sliding-window counter 101.

Measure it

  • See it: a loop of curl -i shows r falling, then 429 with Retry-After; correct is a 200 again after the stated wait.
  • In production: per-tenant 429 rate, limiter store p99, and requests admitted against the downstream's capacity. Steady 429s on normal traffic mean the limit or the capacity is wrong.
  • Bounded by: overload from one caller → per-key limits at the edge, plus load shedding for the total, since per-key limits don't cap the sum.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A rate limiter admits or rejects based on what a caller has already used. The algorithm is a burst decision: token bucket allows bursts, leaky bucket smooths them, and fixed window lets twice the limit through at a boundary. The contract is 429 with Retry-After. The hard part is a correct counter across nodes without a slow dependency on every request.

Q · Mechanism — Walk through the common algorithms and their cost. The Compare table has the summary, so the costs: fixed window is one integer per interval. A sliding log stores a timestamp per request, so 1,000 per minute per client means 1,000 timestamps per client: exact, and expensive. A sliding counter weights the previous window by elapsed time, which removes the boundary burst for two integers, at the cost of being approximate.

Q · Trade-off — 100 requests a minute across 12 nodes. Where does the counter live? Per-node is free and wrong: 1,200 a minute, and dividing by node count breaks on any uneven balancing. Shared storage, such as Redis with an atomic script, is correct and adds a round trip and a dependency to each request. A hybrid keeps a local bucket and syncs near the limit, accepting some overshoot. Fairness tolerates slop; billing quotas and hard ceilings pay for the round trip.

Compare

Token bucket Leaky bucket Fixed window Sliding log Sliding counter
Bursts up to capacity delayed 2× at a boundary none close to none
State per key 2 values queue + time 1 counter N timestamps 2 counters
Accuracy exact for its model exact poor at edges exact approximate
When you'd pick it bursty public APIs shaping egress coarse internal limits small, exact quotas a general default

Pitfalls

  • "A 429 means the client should stop"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's a 4xx, and 4xx usually means "your fault, don't retry".
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it's a retryable failure with a schedule. Treating it as final drops work that would have succeeded.
    ↳ Think instead: wait as told, then retry by the client contract.
  • Not the same: 429 vs 503
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both mean "not now, come back".
    ↳ Difference: 429 scopes the problem to one caller. 503 says the server is unavailable, for everyone.
    ↳ Think instead: quota is 429; capacity is 503, as the tree shows.
  • Don't key limits on IP alone.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it needs no login and it's always there.
    ↳ What goes wrong: one corporate NAT becomes a single caller, while an attacker rotates addresses freely.
    ↳ Do instead: key on tenant or API key, and keep IP as a coarse outer guard.
  • Don't use a limiter as capacity planning.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it stops the graph at a safe line.
    ↳ What goes wrong: if real traffic hits it daily, that's an outage with tidier error messages.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: fix the limit or add capacity, and keep limits for abuse and fairness.
  • Shelf life: the algorithms are durable. The RateLimit draft may change before it's an RFC, and X-RateLimit-* stays common meanwhile.
